opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is actually one of the questions that first pulled me into physics research, so I'm happy to talk about it.

The tension looks very sharp at first. In classical mechanics, chaos means sensitivity to initial conditions. Two trajectories that start extremely close in phase space separate exponentially fast, roughly like e to the lambda t, where lambda is the Lyapunov exponent. That's the butterfly effect.

In quantum mechanics, the Schrödinger equation is linear and the evolution is unitary. If you take two nearby states and measure their distance by the overlap of the wavefunctions, that overlap is exactly conserved. Unitary evolution preserves inner products. So if you naively ask whether two nearby quantum states diverge, the answer is no. Nothing grows exponentially. So where does chaos go?

I think the resolution is that we were asking the wrong question. "Two nearby states" is the wrong object. Classically, the butterfly effect isn't really about two trajectories. It's about how a small perturbation now affects an observable later. You can write that as the derivative of the final position with respect to the initial position, and that's what grows exponentially. Then you translate that into quantum language. A derivative like that becomes, roughly, a commutator between an operator at time zero and an operator at time t, like [W(t), V]. If W(t) is a simple operator and you poke the system with V, at early times they commute because they're unrelated. As time goes on, W(t), in the Heisenberg picture, becomes a more and more complicated operator spread across the whole system, and it stops commuting with V.

So the chaos isn't in the states. It's in the operators. The state evolves linearly, but the operator, if you expand it in a basis of simple local operators, grows. A simple operator becomes a superposition of enormously many complicated ones. People call this operator growth, or scrambling. Information that was local gets spread into very nonlocal correlations, so no simple measurement can recover it, even though in principle it's all still there, because the evolution is unitary.

To diagnose this quantitatively, people use the out-of-time-order correlator, the OTOC. You square the commutator and take an expectation value, which gives correlators with a strange time ordering, like W(t) V W(t) V. In many systems, especially at early times and large N, this deviates from its initial value exponentially, like e to the lambda t, with a quantum Lyapunov exponent. That's how the butterfly effect reappears in quantum mechanics.

There's also a beautiful result by Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford: this quantum Lyapunov exponent has a universal upper bound, 2πk_B T over ħ. A system can't be more chaotic than that. And black holes in Einstein gravity exactly saturate the bound. They're the fastest scramblers in nature. That was a big surprise, and it connected quantum chaos, many-body physics, and quantum gravity through models like SYK. A lot of my own work in that period was around that intersection.

So my short answer is: there isn't really a contradiction. Linearity is about how the full state evolves in a huge Hilbert space. Chaos is about how simple information becomes complicated, how a local operator spreads until it's effectively hidden. The microscopic dynamics can be perfectly linear and reversible while, from the point of view of any observer who can only access simple things, the system looks irreversible and chaotic. Thermalization, the arrow of time, even black hole information loss, all have this flavor: nothing is truly lost, it just becomes too complex to get back.

I find that view quite profound, and in a way it carried over when I moved into AI. A lot of the interesting questions there are also about how simple rules generate enormous complexity, and what an observer with limited resources can extract from it.

r001.rationale: It describes nearby classical trajectories separating exponentially and says the effect of a small initial perturbation on a later position grows exponentially.

r002.rationale: It says unitary evolution preserves inner products and the overlap between nearby states, so their separation does not grow exponentially; this communicates preservation of their angle.

r003.rationale: It identifies the relevant question as how a small perturbation affects a later observable, rather than whether quantum states separate.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I thought about a lot during my PhD, and I think the resolution is actually quite beautiful once you separate what each notion of "chaos" is really measuring.

Classically, the butterfly effect is about trajectories. You take two initial conditions that differ by some tiny amount, you evolve them under the same Hamiltonian, and the separation grows like e to the lambda t. That exponential growth is the Lyapunov exponent. The key point is that classical dynamics in phase space is nonlinear, so nearby points can diverge.

Quantum mechanically, the Schrödinger equation is linear. If I take two states that are close, meaning their overlap is near one, that overlap is exactly preserved under unitary evolution. So there is no divergence of "trajectories" in Hilbert space at all. Taken naively, that seems to say quantum systems cannot be chaotic, which is obviously wrong, because the world is quantum and we see chaos everywhere.

The way I understand it is that the classical question was simply asked in the wrong variables. In the quantum setting you should not perturb the state, you should perturb the dynamics, or equivalently ask how an operator spreads. The object that captures this is the out-of-time-order correlator. You take a local operator W, evolve it in the Heisenberg picture, and ask how much it fails to commute with some other local operator V somewhere else. Initially they commute, because they are far apart. As time goes on, W of t becomes a huge, complicated operator that touches more and more degrees of freedom, and the commutator grows. In the semiclassical limit, that commutator literally reduces to the Poisson bracket, which is the derivative of a late coordinate with respect to an early one, and that is exactly the quantity whose exponential growth defines the classical Lyapunov exponent. So the butterfly effect survives, but it lives in the growth of operators rather than in the separation of states.

Linearity is not in tension with this, because linearity is a statement about superposition of states, whereas chaos is a statement about how information scrambles across many degrees of freedom. A linear map on an exponentially large Hilbert space can be extremely complicated, and the unitary of a chaotic many-body system, viewed in any local basis, is essentially a random matrix. That is really what quantum chaos means: eigenvalue statistics that follow random matrix theory, eigenstates that look thermal, and operators that scramble.

There is one more subtlety I find interesting. The exponential growth of the OTOC is actually only a semiclassical or large-N phenomenon. In a generic lattice spin system you often do not see a clean exponential regime at all. Information spreads ballistically with a butterfly velocity, but the "exponent" is not well defined because there is no small parameter. The cases where you do get a true Lyapunov exponent, like SYK or large-N gauge theories or black holes, are the ones with an emergent semiclassical description, and there you also get the famous bound of two pi times the temperature. So the butterfly effect is in a sense a classical shadow that quantum mechanics reproduces only when there is a classical limit to approach.

So I would say the conflict is apparent rather than real. Quantum mechanics never had chaotic trajectories, but it has something stronger, which is scrambling of quantum information, and the classical butterfly effect is the limit of that when h-bar goes to zero.

r002.rationale: It says unitary evolution preserves the overlap of close states, so their separation does not grow exponentially.

r003.rationale: It points to operator spreading and commutators as the quantum diagnostic, but does not identify changes in local observables as the relevant quantities.

astra-6.text:
I think the apparent conflict comes from using “linear” to describe two different things. Quantum evolution is linear in the wave function: if you superpose two states, their superposition evolves accordingly. The classical butterfly effect concerns how quickly nearby trajectories separate in phase space. Those aren’t directly the same statement.

There is a real distinction, though. If you take two quantum states and evolve them under the same closed-system unitary dynamics, their inner product is preserved. So you don’t get exponential separation in that measure of distance, the way you can for classical trajectories.

But that doesn’t mean quantum systems cannot exhibit chaos. You have to ask a different question—for example, how a perturbation spreads through a system, or how sensitive evolution is to a small change in the Hamiltonian. Those can reveal behavior related to classical chaos even though the underlying evolution remains linear.

In the semiclassical regime, a localized quantum wave packet can approximately follow a classical trajectory for a while. If the classical dynamics are chaotic, that approximation eventually breaks down as the packet spreads and quantum effects become important. So I’d see the butterfly effect as something quantum mechanics can reproduce within a certain regime, rather than something that contradicts quantum linearity.

r001.rationale: It says nearby classical trajectories separate quickly, but does not specify exponential growth from a small initial-condition perturbation.

r002.rationale: It states that unitary evolution preserves the inner product and thus prevents exponential separation in that distance measure, conveying preservation of the states’ angular separation.

r003.rationale: It mentions perturbation spreading and sensitivity to Hamiltonian changes, but does not identify changes in local observables as the relevant quantities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that “sensitivity” can mean different things. In classical chaos, two trajectories that start very close can separate exponentially. In a quantum system, if you evolve two states with the same unitary operator, their inner product is preserved. So their distance in Hilbert space doesn’t grow in that way. You can’t directly transplant the classical picture onto quantum states.

But that doesn’t mean quantum systems can’t be chaotic. You can ask how a small perturbation to the dynamics changes later measurements, or how an initially local disturbance spreads through a many-body system. Those questions can reveal behavior analogous to the butterfly effect, even though the underlying evolution is linear and unitary.

There’s also a distinction between a quantum state and a classical trajectory. In a semiclassical description, a localized wave packet can approximately follow a classical trajectory for some time. Chaotic dynamics can stretch and spread that packet until the single-trajectory approximation stops working. So the apparent conflict comes from treating these two descriptions as if they were the same thing. The interesting question is how classical sensitivity emerges within quantum dynamics, and where that classical description breaks down.

r001.rationale: It says that two classical trajectories starting very close can separate exponentially, describing exponential growth from a small initial difference.

r002.rationale: It states that unitary evolution preserves the inner product and that Hilbert-space distance does not grow in the classical way, conveying preservation of angular separation and no exponential amplification.

r003.rationale: It points to changes in later measurements and spreading local disturbances, but does not identify changes in local observables as the relevant quantity in contrast to separation between quantum states.
